procedural_history.impugned_order: Order by the Lieutenant Governor of Goa to leave India.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The order was challenged in Criminal Revision Petition No. 55 of 1966 at the Judicial Commissioner Court, Goa, Daman and Diu. The petition was dismissed on August 7, 1967.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Rev. Father Monteiro appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the order of the Judicial Commissioner, Goa dated August 7, 1967.

issue.issue_text: Whether the occupation of Goa continued after its annexation by India, thereby making the protections of the Geneva Convention (specifically Articles 47 and 49) available to the appellant against deportation.

facts: The appellant, a resident of Goa, chose to retain his Portuguese nationality after India's annexation of the territory.
He was granted a temporary residential permit to stay in India, which he allowed to expire without seeking renewal.
The Lt. Governor of Goa ordered him to leave India, and he was prosecuted under the Foreigners Act for disobeying this order.
law: The appellant based his defense on Articles 47 and 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention, which was incorporated into Indian law by the Geneva Conventions Act, 1960.
Article 47 states that protected persons in an occupied territory cannot be deprived of the Convention's benefits by any change introduced by the occupation, including annexation.
Article 49 forbids the deportation of protected persons from occupied territory.

The appellant argued that India's military action created an "occupation" that did not end with the unilateral act of annexation, meaning Goa was still an "occupied territory" and he was a "protected person" who could not be deported.
application: The Court first noted a procedural issue: the Geneva Conventions Act does not grant a specific right for an individual to sue the government for enforcement of the Conventions. It creates an obligation for the government but does not provide a cause of action for protected persons.
On the main issue, the Court distinguished between a "premature annexation" during an ongoing conflict and a "true annexation" following complete conquest and subjugation.
The Court reasoned that Article 47's protection against annexation only applies to premature annexations, not to a completed conquest.

In Goa's case, the military action was swift, lasting only a few hours with no resistance. The annexation followed so closely upon the military action that it constituted a "true annexation by conquest and subjugation," which was complete on December 20, 1961.
Because the annexation was complete and lawful, the "occupation" in the sense used by the Geneva Conventions ceased on that date.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that the occupation of Goa ended with its complete annexation and subjugation by India on December 20, 1961. Therefore, the protections of the Geneva Convention, including the prohibition on deportation under Article 49, ceased to apply from that date. As a foreigner who had overstayed his permit, the appellant was subject to the Foreigners Act and was rightly prosecuted for disobeying the order to leave India.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Foreigners Act and orders passed thereunder could be legally applied to the appellant, who had chosen Portuguese nationality, to order his deportation.

facts: The appellant, a resident of Goa, chose to retain his Portuguese nationality after India's annexation of the territory.
This decision made him a foreigner in India.
He was granted a temporary residential permit, which he allowed to expire without seeking renewal.
He was subsequently ordered to leave India under the Foreigners Act and was prosecuted for disobeying that order.
law: The Court invoked the 'cardinal principle of international law' that every sovereign state has territorial supremacy.
This supremacy grants a state the legal right and competence to control the reception, residence, and exclusion of aliens (foreigners) from its territory.
A state can therefore make laws to regulate the entry, residence, and eviction of aliens.
application: Because the appellant chose to be a Portuguese national, he was legally classified as an alien in India.
As an alien, his right to remain in the country was not absolute but was subject to India's laws governing foreigners.
Therefore, the Indian government was legally competent to apply the Foreigners Act and related orders to him.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the Foreigners Act was legally applicable to the appellant. As a foreigner by his own choice, he could only stay in India with a valid permit. Since he overstayed his permit and disobeyed a lawful deportation order, his prosecution and conviction under the Act were correct.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the occupation of Goa continued after its annexation by India, thereby making the protections of the Geneva Convention (specifically Articles 47 and 49) available to the appellant against deportation.
appellant_arguments: The Geneva Conventions have become part of Indian law.
Under International Law (specifically the UN Charter), the acquisition of territory by force does not confer title.
India's constitutional amendment only legalized the annexation internally. In International Law, the territory remained 'occupied' because it was neither ceded nor had the occupying power withdrawn.
Therefore, the protections of Articles 47 and 49 of the Geneva Convention continued to be available to the appellant.
respondent_arguments: Occupation means belligerent occupation by armed forces, and it ends with conquest followed by subjugation.
The Geneva Conventions ceased to apply after December 20, 1961.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Foreigners Act and orders passed thereunder could be legally applied to the appellant, who had chosen Portuguese nationality, to order his deportation.
appellant_arguments: As a person protected by the Geneva Conventions in an occupied territory, the appellant could not be deported and therefore committed no offense by disobeying the deportation order.
respondent_arguments: The appellant was offered Indian nationality but refused it, choosing to retain his Portuguese nationality.
As a Portuguese national, he was a foreigner in India and required a permit to stay.
He failed to renew his temporary residential permit.
Therefore, he was rightly prosecuted under the Foreigners Act for disobeying the order to leave India.

statutes.principle: As a legally competent law for a state to regulate the entry, residence, and eviction of aliens, and under which the appellant was validly prosecuted for disobeying a deportation order.
As a legally competent law for a state, exercising its territorial supremacy, to regulate aliens within its territory.
As the source of the Lt. Governor of Goa's authority to order the appellant to leave India.
The Court interpreted the Act and concluded that it gives no specific right to an individual to approach a municipal court to challenge a deportation order.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Every state, by reason of its territorial supremacy, has the discretionary legal right and competence to exclude aliens and regulate their entry, residence, and eviction. The Geneva Conventions Act does not create a cause of action for a private individual to enforce the Conventions in a municipal court against the government.
obiter: It was not necessary to decide the question of whether deportation was an Act of State against which municipal courts could give no remedy.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Geneva Conventions ceased to apply to Goa after its conquest and subjugation by India on December 20, 1961. The appellant, having refused Indian nationality and chosen to remain a Portuguese national, became a foreigner in Indian territory. As such, he was subject to the Foreigners Act, and the state possessed the sovereign right, based on the principle of territorial supremacy, to regulate his residence and order his deportation.
legal_tests_applied: A territory is considered occupied when it finds itself in fact placed under the authority of a hostile army, and the laws of belligerent occupation apply only during the course of actual warfare; they do not apply to an occupation that follows the total defeat of the enemy.
The principle of territorial supremacy grants every state the discretion and legal right to exclude aliens from all or any part of its territory.
Occupation by armed forces comes to an end by conquest followed by subjugation.
why_appellant_lost: The Geneva Conventions ceased to apply after December 20, 1961, as the occupation ended with the conquest and subjugation of the territory.
The appellant chose to refuse Indian nationality and retain his Portuguese nationality, thereby making himself a foreigner subject to Indian laws governing aliens.

The Geneva Conventions Act only creates an obligation for the Government of India to respect the conventions; it does not create an enforceable right or cause of action for a protected person in a municipal court.
The appellant's argument overlooked the cardinal principle of international law that the reception and residence of an alien is a matter of discretion for every state.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the state's argument that occupation means belligerent occupation by armed forces and that it ends with conquest followed by subjugation.
As a Portuguese national who refused the offer of Indian citizenship, the appellant was a foreigner who could only stay in India by taking out a permit.
Every state has the legal right and competence, by reason of its own territorial supremacy, to exclude aliens and make laws regulating their entry, residence, and eviction.
The application of the Foreigners Act and orders passed under it to the appellant, who had chosen Portuguese nationality, was legally competent.
policy_considerations: If there is no provision of law which the courts can enforce, the court may be powerless and may have to leave the matter to what Westlake aptly described as indignation of mankind.
The reception and residence of an alien is a matter of discretion for every state.
A state exercises territorial supremacy over all persons in its territory, whether its own subjects or aliens.
